learn.hook: If you measure a table with your handspan and your little brother measures it with his, you'll get different answers. Who is right?
points: Long ago people measured length with body parts: handspan, cubit (elbow to fingertip), foot, pace (step) and angul (finger width). In ancient India, units like angul and dhanush were used.
Body measures differ from person to person, so the same object gives different results.
So the world agreed on standard units. The SI unit (International System of Units) of length is the metre (m).
1 metre (m) = 100 centimetres (cm); 1 centimetre = 10 millimetres (mm); 1 kilometre (km) = 1000 metres.
We choose the unit to suit the length: mm for a pencil tip, cm for a book, m for a room, km for the distance between cities.

example.q: Tanvi's ribbon is 2 m 35 cm long. How long is it in centimetres?
steps: 1 m = 100 cm, so 2 m = 200 cm.
Add the extra 35 cm: 200 + 35.

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers measure cloth in metres, road signs show distances in kilometres, and your school ruler shows centimetres and millimetres.

quiz.q: What is the SI unit of length?
quiz.explain: The metre is the standard (SI) unit of length. Centimetre and kilometre are made from it.
steps: The world agreed on standard units of length.
The SI unit of length is the metre (m).
Centimetre and kilometre are made from the metre; handspan is a body measure.
So the SI unit is the metre.
Answer: Metre
quiz.mistake: Picks a smaller or bigger unit instead of the base SI unit

quiz.q: Why are handspans not good for measuring accurately?
options: Different people have different handspan lengths
Handspans are not allowed in India
quiz.explain: Each person's handspan is a different length, so results do not match.
steps: Body measures differ from person to person.
Two people's handspans give different results for the same object.
So handspans are not accurate because different people have different handspan lengths.
Answer: Different people have different handspan lengths
quiz.mistake: Does not see the problem of non-standard units

quiz.q: How many centimetres are there in 4 m?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by 10 or 1000 instead of 100
steps: Answer: 400 cm

quiz.q: How many millimetres are in 7 cm?
quiz.explain: 1 cm = 10 mm, so 7 cm = 7 × 10 = 70 mm.
quiz.mistake: Uses 100 instead of 10 for cm to mm
steps: 1 cm = 10 mm
Answer: 70 mm

quiz.q: Ravi's school is 3 km from home. How far is that in metres?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by 100 instead of 1000
steps: Answer: 3000 m

quiz.q: Which unit is best to measure the length of a pencil?
quiz.explain: A pencil is about 15 to 20 cm long, so centimetres suit it best.
steps: Choose the unit to suit the length.
A pencil is about 15 to 20 cm long.
Kilometre and metre are far too big; mm is for very tiny lengths like a pencil tip.
So the centimetre is best.
Answer: Centimetre
quiz.mistake: Does not match the unit size to the object

quiz.q: Which old unit is the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger?
quiz.explain: A cubit is measured from the elbow to the fingertip.
steps: Old body units: handspan, cubit, foot, pace, angul.
The cubit is from the elbow to the fingertip.
So the answer is cubit.
Answer: Cubit
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the names of body measures

quiz.q: A rope is 1 m 50 cm long. How many centimetres is that?
quiz.mistake: Writes the numbers side by side instead of converting
steps: Answer: 150 cm

teach.ask: Gappu measures a twig with his tiny claw: 'It's 12 claws long! But my friend the crow says it's 5 claws. Who's right?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Claws and handspans are different for everyone. Using a standard unit like the metre means everyone gets the same answer!
teach.nudge: Why do our claw measurements differ? What unit should we both use?

revise.summary: Body measures like handspan and cubit differ from person to person, so the world uses standard units. The SI unit of length is the metre; we pick mm, cm, m or km to suit the length.
focus: Why body measures are not reliable
Converting between mm, cm, m and km
Choosing a suitable unit for an object
remember: Cubit = elbow to fingertip; angul = finger width
traps: Don't call the centimetre the SI unit; it is the metre.
Don't use km for small objects like a pencil; use cm.

learn.hook: A ruler is only as good as the person using it. A tiny slip of the eye can change your answer!
points: Place the scale along the length of the object, touching it.
Start from the zero mark. If the zero mark is broken, start from another full mark (like 1 cm) and subtract it from the final reading.
Keep your eye directly above the point you are reading. Looking from the side gives a wrong reading.
To measure a curved line, lay a thread along it, mark the ends, straighten the thread and measure it with a scale.
Choose the right tool: a ruler for a book, a measuring tape for your waist or a tree trunk, a metre scale for a door.

example.q: Sameer's ruler has a broken edge, so he places a pencil starting at the 2.0 cm mark. The other end is at 11.5 cm. How long is the pencil?
steps: The pencil starts at 2.0 cm, not at 0.
Length = end reading − start reading.

learn.reallife: Tailors use a soft measuring tape around your shoulders and waist, and carpenters use a metal tape to measure wood before cutting.

games.title: How to measure a curved line
items: Place a thread along the curved line
Mark where the line starts and ends on the thread
Straighten the thread
Measure the thread between the marks with a ruler

items.text: Keep your eye ___ above the mark you are reading.
To measure your waist, use a ___.
If the zero mark is broken, ___ the starting reading from the end reading.
To measure a curved line, we can use a ___.

quiz.q: Where should your eye be when you read a scale?
options: To the left of the mark
To the right of the mark
quiz.explain: Looking from the side makes the mark seem shifted, giving a wrong reading.
steps: Looking from the side makes the mark seem shifted.
This gives a wrong reading.
So keep your eye directly above the mark.
Answer: Directly above the mark
quiz.mistake: Does not know that viewing angle changes the reading

quiz.q: A leaf starts at 1.0 cm and ends at 7.5 cm on a ruler. What is its length?
quiz.mistake: Reads only the end mark and forgets to subtract the start
steps: End − start
Answer: 6.5 cm

quiz.q: Which tool is best to measure around the trunk of a mango tree?
quiz.explain: A flexible measuring tape can wrap around a curved trunk.
steps: A tree trunk is curved.
A flexible measuring tape can wrap around it.
A 15 cm ruler is stiff and too short.
So use a measuring tape.
Answer: A measuring tape
quiz.mistake: Chooses a stiff ruler for a curved surface

quiz.q: How can you measure the length of a curved line on a map?
options: Lay a thread along it and then measure the thread
Measure only the start and end points
quiz.explain: The thread follows every curve. When straightened, its length can be read on a ruler.
steps: A ruler cannot bend along a curve.
Lay a thread along the curved line and mark its ends.
Straighten the thread and measure it with a scale.
So lay a thread along it and then measure the thread.
Answer: Lay a thread along it and then measure the thread
quiz.mistake: Measures only the straight distance between the ends

quiz.q: Kriti's ruler has a broken zero, so she starts measuring her eraser at the 3 cm mark. The eraser ends at 8 cm. How long is it?
quiz.explain: Length = 8 − 3 = 5 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds the readings or reads only the end mark
steps: End − start
Answer: 5 cm

quiz.q: Why should the scale touch the object along its length?
options: So the scale does not get dirty
quiz.explain: If the scale is lifted or tilted, the marks do not line up with the ends of the object.
steps: The scale should be placed along the object, touching it.
If it is lifted or tilted, the marks do not line up with the ends.
So it must touch the object so the reading is accurate.
Answer: So the reading is accurate
quiz.mistake: Thinks placement of the scale does not affect the reading

quiz.q: Ayaan measures a book and gets 24.5 cm. What does the '.5' mean?
quiz.explain: Each centimetre has 10 mm, so 0.5 cm = 5 mm. The book is 24 cm and 5 mm long.
steps: 1 cm = 10 mm, so 0.5 cm = 5 mm.
= 24 cm and 5 mm
So '.5' means 5 millimetres more than 24 cm.
Answer: 5 millimetres more than 24 cm
quiz.mistake: Does not connect decimal centimetres with millimetres

quiz.q: Which is a correct way to measure the length of a classroom?
options: Count your steps once and guess
Use a long measuring tape laid straight along the floor
Use a 15 cm ruler only once
quiz.explain: A long tape laid straight gives an accurate measurement of a big length.
steps: A classroom is a big length, measured in metres.
A long measuring tape laid straight gives an accurate result.
Steps vary, a short ruler adds errors, and a clock measures time.
So use a long measuring tape laid straight along the floor.
Answer: Use a long measuring tape laid straight along the floor
quiz.mistake: Uses a non-standard or unsuitable method

teach.ask: Gappu squints at a ruler from the side: 'My crayon is 8 cm! No wait, 8.3! Why does it keep changing?'
teach.praise: Got it! Keep the scale along the crayon, start at zero (or subtract the start) and look straight down. Now my reading won't wobble!
teach.nudge: Where should I keep my eyes? And where should I start measuring from?

revise.summary: To measure correctly, lay the scale along the object, start from zero (or subtract the start mark), keep your eye directly above the mark, and use a thread for curved lines.
focus: Steps for reading a scale correctly
Measuring with a broken scale by subtracting the start mark
Measuring curved lines with a thread
Choosing the right tool: ruler, measuring tape, metre scale
remember: Keep your eye directly above the mark you read
Broken zero: start at a full mark and subtract it from the end reading
Curved line: thread along it, straighten, then measure
traps: Don't read the scale from the side; it gives a wrong reading.
Don't forget to subtract the starting mark when the zero is broken.
Don't use a stiff ruler for a tree trunk; use a measuring tape.

learn.hook: A cricket ball flies, a fan spins, a swing goes back and forth. Everything is moving, but in different ways!
points: An object is in motion if its position changes with time compared to its surroundings; otherwise it is at rest.
Linear motion: moving along a straight line, like a train on a straight track, a falling stone, or a sprinter in a 100 m race.
Circular motion: moving along a circle around a centre, like the tip of a fan blade, a giant wheel at a mela, or a stone tied to a string and whirled.
Periodic motion: a motion that repeats itself after fixed intervals of time, like a swinging pendulum, a jhula going to and fro, or the hands of a clock.
Some motions are of more than one type. A fan blade moves in a circle and repeats again and again, so it is both circular and periodic.

example.q: What type of motion does a child on a swing (jhula) have?
steps: The swing goes forward and comes back to the same point.
It repeats this to-and-fro movement again and again, taking about the same time for each swing.
A motion that repeats after fixed time intervals is periodic.

learn.reallife: At a Dussehra or Diwali mela you can spot all three: a toy train on a straight track (linear), a giant wheel (circular) and a pendulum-like boat ride swinging to and fro (periodic).

games.title: Motion check
items: A train moving on a straight track shows linear motion.
It moves along a straight line.
A swinging pendulum shows periodic motion.
It repeats its to-and-fro movement after fixed intervals.
The tip of a ceiling fan blade moves in a straight line.
It moves in a circle around the centre of the fan.
The hands of a clock show periodic motion.
They come back to the same position after fixed times.
A book lying on a table is in motion with respect to the table.
Its position is not changing compared to the table, so it is at rest.

quiz.q: A stone dropped from a building shows which type of motion?
quiz.explain: The stone falls straight down, along a straight line.
steps: Linear motion is motion along a straight line.
A dropped stone falls straight down.
So it shows linear motion.
Answer: Linear
quiz.mistake: Confuses straight-line motion with other types

quiz.q: Which is an example of circular motion?
options: A car on a straight highway
A giant wheel turning at a mela
A toy train on a straight track
quiz.explain: The seats of a giant wheel move in a circle around its centre.
steps: Circular motion is moving along a circle around a centre.
The seats of a giant wheel go round its centre.
Cars, balls and trains on straight paths show linear motion.
So the giant wheel shows circular motion.
Answer: A giant wheel turning at a mela
quiz.mistake: Does not identify movement around a centre

quiz.q: What is periodic motion?
options: Motion that repeats after fixed intervals of time
Motion only in a straight line
quiz.explain: Periodic motion repeats itself regularly, like a pendulum or a clock's hands.
steps: Periodic motion repeats itself.
It repeats after fixed intervals of time, like a pendulum or clock hands.
So it is motion that repeats after fixed intervals of time.
Answer: Motion that repeats after fixed intervals of time
quiz.mistake: Thinks periodic means straight-line motion

quiz.q: A swinging pendulum shows:
quiz.explain: A pendulum moves to and fro, repeating after equal intervals of time.
steps: A pendulum swings to and fro.
Each swing repeats after an equal interval of time.
So it shows periodic motion.
Answer: Periodic motion
quiz.mistake: Thinks to-and-fro motion is linear

quiz.q: The tip of a ceiling fan blade moves in a circle and repeats. Its motion is:
quiz.explain: It moves around a circle and returns to the same point again and again, so it is circular and periodic.
steps: The fan tip moves around a circle → circular.
It returns to the same point again and again at regular times → periodic.
So its motion is both circular and periodic.
Answer: Both circular and periodic
quiz.mistake: Thinks a motion can only be of one type

quiz.q: A girl sitting in a moving bus is at rest compared to which of these?
quiz.explain: Her position does not change compared to her seat, but it changes compared to things outside.
steps: An object is at rest if its position does not change compared to its surroundings.
The girl's position does not change compared to her seat.
It does change compared to the trees, road and houses outside.
So she is at rest compared to her seat in the bus.
Answer: Her seat in the bus
quiz.mistake: Does not understand that motion is compared with surroundings

quiz.q: A sprinter running in a 100 m race on a straight track shows:
quiz.explain: On a straight track, the runner moves along a straight line.
steps: The sprinter runs along a straight track.
Motion along a straight line is linear motion.
So the sprinter shows linear motion.
Answer: Linear motion
quiz.mistake: Confuses straight running with other motions

quiz.q: Which of these shows periodic motion?
options: A car moving on a straight road
A ball dropped from a roof
A stone lying on the ground
quiz.explain: A vibrating string moves to and fro again and again, so its motion is periodic.
steps: Periodic motion repeats again and again.
A plucked sitar string vibrates to and fro repeatedly.
A car on a straight road and a dropped ball show linear motion; a lying stone is at rest.
So the vibrating sitar string shows periodic motion.
Answer: A plucked sitar string vibrating
quiz.mistake: Does not recognise vibration as repeating motion

teach.ask: Gappu watches a fan, a swing and a train: 'They are all moving, but they look so different! What kinds of motion are there?'
teach.praise: Wheee! Straight line is linear, going round is circular, and repeating to and fro is periodic. I spin, I swing, I glide!
teach.nudge: What do we call a motion that goes round and round? And one that repeats back and forth?

revise.summary: An object is in motion if its position changes with time compared to its surroundings. Motion can be linear (straight line), circular (around a centre) or periodic (repeating), and sometimes more than one type.
focus: Rest and motion compared to surroundings
Recognising linear, circular and periodic motion
Objects with more than one type of motion
remember: Linear: along a straight line (falling stone, sprinter)
Circular: along a circle around a centre (giant wheel, fan tip)
Periodic: repeats after fixed intervals (pendulum, jhula, clock hands)
A fan blade is both circular and periodic
traps: Rest and motion depend on what you compare with: a girl in a bus is at rest compared to her seat.
Don't call a pendulum's motion circular; it is periodic (to and fro).
